title: Robot Framework Test Automation: Automate Web, Desktop, Mobile, and Embedded Systems
text: What makes Robot Framework flexible enough to test medical devices, low code bots, monitoring systems, and embedded hardware, all with one framework? In this RoboCon 2027 special, Joe Colantonio talks with four leaders in the Robot Framework community: Lydia Peabody, Kelby Stine, Simon Meggle, and Linda Van De Vooren. They talk about why Robot Framework’s library ecosystem lets you test far beyond the browser, and how AI and the Robot Framework MCP server are speeding up test creation. They also explain why human knowledge still matters when tests break. You’ll hear how the official style guide came together, how RoboCon’s first program committee built the 2027 lineup, and the community stories that turned attendees into speakers, ambassadors, and organizers. In this episode you’ll learn: RoboCon 2027 runs in Helsinki, March 8 to 12, and online, April 7 to 9. Joe is hosting online again and attending in person for the first time. Register now: https://testgld.link/robocon27

title: Inference engineering for software engineers
author: Gergely Orosz
text: A recent trend we’ve covered is of tech companies moving to open models to rein in AI spend: Uber cut its per-token costs by 50%, Pinterest by 90%, and even AT&T has achieved a 56% decrease. But how do you move from a frontier lab’s APIs to using open models? There are two options: “Bare metal:” With plenty of time and money, you can go “bare metal” and purchase a few dozen NVIDIA GPUs and use those AI supercomputers, like Revolut has done : running 56 separate B200 units itself to serve its inference needs. This is a lot of work to set it up, but after that, operational costs are as cheap as it gets. Inference provider: most companies contract with an inference provider that operates large fleets of GPUs, and makes it easy for customers to onboard and start using open models fast. Onboarding to an inference provider to run LLM workloads comes with challenges, such as dealing with tail latencies, worrying about cache hit rates, rate limits, and more. Inference engineering is a set of engineering practices that we believe is increasingly beneficial for software engineers to familiarize themselves with. To go deeper into this area, we’ve talked with three leading inference providers to learn more: Modal , Fireworks AI , and Baseten . Today, we cover: What are inference providers & how do they differ from AI labs? They have GPU infrastructure similar to frontier labs, don’t train their own frontier models and are experts at hosting open models. When to switch from frontier labs? The most common reasons are to reduce costs, have more control over latency, and to fine-tune AI models. Choosing a model, provider, and deployment strategy. Use evals to find the right open model for your use case, evaluate vendors, and decide between multi-tenant API usage and dedicated GPUs. Stage #1: API replacement using a multi-tenant inference setup . The easiest way to onboard to an inference provider is to “swap” the API of a frontier lab to an API of an inference provider. But there may be latency problems and caching issues at high loads. Signs you’ve outgrown multi-tenant inference APIs. Hitting rate limits, performance consistency problems, and overpaying for usage are signs that it might be time to adopt dedicated GPUs. Stage #2: Configuring dedicated GPU nodes. With dedicated GPUs, you’ll need to get into the details: size of the model, interactivity versus throughput, KV cache sizing, failover options, and more. Speculative decoding. If there’s unused compute during the decode phase, you might consider a Speculator to further boost inference performance. As usual, we have no affiliation with vendors mentioned in this article, and have not been paid to mention any company. Special thanks to Richard Gong (Inference lead, Modal), Dmytro Dzhulgakov (cofounder and CTO, Fireworks), and Philip Kiely (Special Projects at Baseten) for sharing details about inference engineering challenges. 1. What are inference providers & how do they differ from AI labs? Inference providers are companies that sell access to LLMs which they run on users’ behalf. From the outside, this isn’t so different to what OpenAI and Anthropic offer: an API endpoint, ability to stream tokens, and pay based on token usage. But what makes inference providers different from frontier labs is the models running behind the endpoint: inference providers run open-weight models, whereas frontier labs train their own models. In this field, Modal, Fireworks, and Baseten each operate slightly different strategies: Modal sees itself as a cloud infrastructure provider that focuses on making its offering programmable via its SDKs. It natively supports inference services through its SDKs, but leans heavily on the open source ecosystem for running its inference workloads efficiently. Performance tweaks to its stack are merged upstream. In the words of Richard Gong, Inference Lead at Modal: “when you run code on Modal, you should be able to see all the code that’s running.” Fireworks positions

title: External sandboxes for coding agents
text: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running: I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches. title: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol
text: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol OpenAI: We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. They're available in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol . I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models. 6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions. GPT-6.2 Sol is the same $2/$10 price as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol - which are half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol ($4/$20). Here are the pelicans for GPT-6.2 Sol and for GPT-6.2 Astra . The 6.2 Astra max pelican looks like this: I have a full comparison grid here , but here's how the high/xhigh/max pelicans compare with the previous Sol and Astra releases: I also ran my most recent benchmark prompt against the two models, using "Ultra' effort levels in the Codex CLI: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's Sol and here's Astra . Neither of them did a good enough job of morphing Yonkers into a big mech, at least in comparison to Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon . This video showing the Astra and Sol animations playing out at the same time: I created that video using GPT-6.2 Astra (Ultra) in the Codex desktop app by prompting: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-astra-ultra/index.html and https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-sol-ultra/index.html are two videos of the same thing by two different models I need a video of the first 10 seconds where the top half of the video plays the first and the bottom half plays the second I need an overlaid label of "GPT-6.2 Astra" on the top half and "GPT-6.2 Sol" on the bottom half. These labels should be tastefully positioned. Make the video square and 2000x2000 pixels Then later: OK make it 20s Here's the exported transcript . The buzz around these new models is mixed at the moment. Astra 6.2 isn't scoring quite as high as Fable 5.2 on various benchmarks, and I've seen a few complaints that its communication style can be confusing. Theo Browne's review (in the form of a feedback letter he sent OpenAI during pre-release) has this useful example: When this model is working on long tasks, it can pull in a lot of subagents and manage them pretty well. It will then proceed to randomly ask you some weird internal implementation detail bullshit that you could not under any earthly circumstance understand, much less have input on . I sent "/goal make a new level for Outer Wilds". 2 hours in, it's "blocked" because it wanted to ask me "does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?" title: Green Tests, Wrong Answers
author: Alan Page
text: Disclosure: SmartBear sponsored this post. The opinions are mine. I was hanging out with a friend of mine a few weeks ago. He was well respected in tech for a long time, and is retired (mostly) now. When I met him for a beer, he was chatting with a small business owner who was telling him about setting up her online store. Her store had a pretty simple shipping rule: orders over $50 ship free. The owner, Dana, used AI to add the rule to the checkout code, and it wrote a set of tests along with it. AI wrote the tests, and every test passed. For as long as I’ve been in software, product requirements have been ambiguous and incomplete. As you’d expect, this ended up being true with Dana as well. There was no rule on whether the $50 was measured before or after any coupons or other discounts, so a $60 cart with a 20 percent coupon, which came to $48, shipped free. When writing the code, AI filled in made up gaps about when to apply a shipping discount, and the tests made the same assumptions. It wasn’t a huge issue, but the shop covered shipping on those orders for over a month before she eventually spotted it in the books. Application Integrity SmartBear uses the term application integrity for how teams maintain confidence that their applications work as intended. I like the name because it states what we’re ultimately after, which is confidence, and a passing test suite doesn’t always give us the confidence we’re looking for. I’ve said for a long time that quality is a property of the whole system of people, practices, and tools - and integrity works the same way. Tooling has always accelerated whatever culture is already in place, and that includes agentic development. Agentic code development is changing how we calculate confidence. Code is written faster than anyone can read it, so reviewing the code stops being a realistic way to know it works. That leaves behavior as the thing we need to check, and that means more focus on whether the running application does what the people using it actually need. Validation I’ve heard from SmartBear that they’re seeing teams build in-house solutions with AI without the end-to-end functional testing they need for release confidence. This is something I see a lot in my own conversations as well when talking with different teams, and I’m not at all surprised. When the same AI writes the code and the tests from the same assumptions, both come from the same reading of the requirements and share the same data and ambiguous sources. Dana’s tests passed because they completely agreed with the code. I’ve taught 100s of developers to be good testers, and I fully believe developers are perfectly capable of testing their own code well. AI can be really good at both building and testing successfully, but it needs the right guardrails and guidance to be successful at it. Unfortunately, most people don’t bother to set up context and skills thoroughly. They ask the AI to create tests and accept whatever comes back, which is how Dana ended up with a test suite that agreed with her code, yet provided no value. Good guardrails can be simple. Things like acceptance criteria written into the prompt before creating code, instructions to list every ambiguous requirement and ask about them before building, or a rule that tests should validate behavior or not code are all helpful. I especially want to see the running application behave as intended from the outside, because that test tells you whether the guardrails worked. Dana’s checkout shows both. A guardrail that asked the AI to list open questions would have surfaced the coupon rule before any code existed, and a check of the running shop from a customer’s point of view would have caught it quickly, because customers like to use coupons and discounts. The validator brings expectations that the builder never had. BearQ BearQ is SmartBear’s QA agent, and I think it’s a pretty good example of this kind of independent test. title: Focus on finishing
author: Jit Gosai
text: I was talking to a team about improving their metrics, and it got me thinking about how we could encourage better ways of working without making the numbers themselves the goal. It reminded me of a simple principle we used to follow: focus on finishing . It was a really simple concept. It didn’t require any special policies, practices, tools, training or workshops. It just needed everyone in the team to agree. What does focusing on finishing look like? The idea was simple: before starting something new, look at what you can help finish. Rather than picking up another piece of work, check in with your colleagues. Does anyone need help finishing something they’re already working on? It’s not necessarily about doing the work for them. It’s about supporting them, removing blockers and helping work move towards completion. Every stand-up becomes an opportunity to look at what we can finish, rather than what we can start. You can take this further by looking at how you slice work. Smaller pieces of work are generally easier to finish, and they allow you to get feedback sooner. If you’re working in sprints, you pull in less work initially and add more if you have the capacity. Throughout the sprint, the focus is on completing work rather than starting more and carrying it over into the next sprint. This also starts to shift the team’s behaviour away from individually completing their own work and towards taking collective responsibility for getting things finished. Over time, people stop asking “How do I get my work finished?” and start asking “How do we get this across the line?” This can help build a more collaborative team, where people support one another, share knowledge and learn together. What are the benefits? This one principle can have quite a few benefits. Better flow. Rather than having lots of partially finished work sitting around, you’re focusing on getting work across the line. With less work in progress, you’re also likely to see improvements in cycle times and potentially lead times too More stability and flexibility. You’re also creating the potential for some slack in the system. If unexpected work arrives, or something you’ve shipped comes back because of an issue, you’ve potentially got more capacity to deal with it without constantly interrupting other work. More opportunities for continuous improvement. Rather than constantly focusing on starting and delivering the next thing, teams could use the extra time to look at how they can do things better. Not just faster, but more efficiently and simply. What does finished actually mean? This principle usually leads people to ask, what does finished actually mean? Well, finished can be completing a ticket . For instance, you’ve written the code, carried out some testing and closed the ticket. It can be delivering something . For instance, the code is integrated into the wider product, deployed, and users can start using the new functionality. Finished could also mean delivering value . For instance, the feature is achieving some business outcome, e.g. driving sign-ups or increasing engagement. And the time scales on which these different measures of finished can vary too. With completing a ticket taking anything from a couple of hours to a few days, and delivering value taking anywhere between a few days to a few months. So how far does a team’s responsibility for finishing extend? Having a shared understanding of what finished means helps the team know what they’re working towards. But it also encourages us to think beyond simply completing tasks and consider whether the things we’re delivering are actually creating the value we hoped for. Why this matters even more with agentic engineering Our ability to start work is going to go through the roof. AI agents are making it easier and quicker than ever to generate code, create features and start new pieces of work. title: Launch HN: StarSling (YC P25) – Self-improving CI for agent-volume repos
author: yonasb
text: We’re Yonas and Daniel and we’re building StarSling ( https://starsling.dev ), fast GitHub Actions runners with AI agents that ship PRs to continuously improve your tests and workflows. Every CI job gets its own ephemeral sandbox on the fastest Zen 5 machines and NVMe Disk with unlimited concurrency so a burst of agent PRs all run at once. We’re different from other runners because ours come with agents that cut down your CI bill over time. PRs are generated through our CI harness, which runs an agent loop that’s tuned to improve your CI speed and reduce cost. Mastra now merges over 1,800 PRs a month and we got their slowest workflow from 29m 56s on GitHub-hosted runners down to 5m 06s (5.87x) on StarSling. We realized the true value of having an agent loop running on top of fast runners when our agents found an 11-month-old performance bottleneck in better-auth. The fix made one of their test jobs 5.4x faster: https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/10762 . I previously founded StackShare, which grew to over 1.5M developers. Daniel helped build Netflix's internal developer portal. Last year we started building AI agents for DevOps because shipping code to prod fell way behind agentic coding. We hit the CI bottleneck ourselves as we were building agents. Our own agents shipped so many PRs that at peak our job queues were backed up for hours and our CI bill got close to our inference bill. We now support per-second billing, and just shipped StarSling Disks - persistent disks that give you a 4.9x speedup in dependencies ready over actions/cache. You can see a quick demo of disks in action here : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2JrrpRm9Mww . Our CI harness runs a loop that has agents: - Analyze your workflows, run logs, and machine telemetry - Propose an optimization - Test your unchanged workflow side by side the proposed change - Deterministically judge that the difference is statistically significant - Ship the winner to you as a PR with benchmarks evidence We benchmarked open source repos on our runners and average 10x speedup in wall clock time with 70% less runner time: - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-gogs (12.8x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-shellcheck (5.5x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-chatwoot (3.9x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-transfer.sh (11.7x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-mirotalksfu (36.4x) Yes, you can do these optimizations yourself with prompts so we’ve released skills for this: https://github.com/starslingdev/skills . The benefit of using our agents is that you don’t need to spend tokens and CI compute finding optimizations yourself. We started building our runners on AWS at the beginning of the year and realized that was too expensive. But at that time there weren’t any cloud providers that could give us the same machines we were getting on AWS, billed per minute (microVMs). So we convinced a handful of sandbox providers to get Zen 5s and started benchmarking them publicly ( https://github.com/starslingdev/hpc-sandbox-benchmarks ). We’ve learned that fast infrastructure is table stakes for CI, but it’s not sufficient on its own. To get fast and cost effective CI you need a process that continues making improvements. We turned CI optimizations from OpenAI, Anthropic, Linear and others into playbooks for your agent: https://starsling.dev/ci-playbooks . To try it, give your agent this URL: https://docs.starsling.dev/start . You get 2,000 free minutes. Our agents start opening PRs once you've hit about 10,000 minutes. Today we announced our CI Challenge: if StarSling can't save you at least 10% on your next CI bill, we'll literally give you $1,000. Eligibility and rules here: https://starsling.dev/blog/ci-challenge . We’d love your feedback on the headless experience and what you’d like to see improved in your own CI setup!

title: Show HN: TrnRT – An open-source LLM inference engine for AWS Trainium
author: sanchitmonga22
text: Hi HN, Sanchit here from RunAnywhere (YC W26). We just open-sourced TrnRT: Trainium RunTime, our inference engine for AWS Trainium. We started 3 weeks back, and currently we’re able to serve and run GLM 5.3 flash (FP8) on AWS trn2.48xlarge, and will bring more models support soon. It’s open to contributions :) What it does today: - Serves 2 instances of GLM-5.3 flash on a single box, 8 trn2 with a cache aware router. - Can process 3.57M TPM (tokens per minute) on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks. - Runs decode as one NKI kernel per layer half, or for the 11 sparse-attention layers fuses both blocks into a single kernel, for faster performance. We started working on Trn2 because we wanted to explore it and see if we can come close to beating it’s performance in terms of cost efficiency compared to H100/H200. A big MoE with 1M context window such as GLM-5.3 flash requires a lot of memory, and memory/tb on a trn2.48xlarge costs less than half compared to 8x h200 on AWS, and hence we wanted to experiment with it and now we’re sharing some early results. But AWS's own stack didn't support the model: vLLM Neuron's latest release did not register any GLM model, and NxDI, AWS's own distributed inference framework, is no longer under active development. We also saw the drop of SGLang Neuron implementation yesterday, but there is no good support for Trn2, which is the only chip available for public use right now. We ran semiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks, which replays real coding agent sessions: - 1 box served 28.9 RPM(requests per minute) with 32 agents at batch 12 (also known as concurrency) -The P50 TTFT with a cached prompt at 16 agents is ~1.24 seconds with a decode of 35.9 tps. Initially, the recurrence in one kda (linear attention) layer was ~2% of the layer's attention time at batch 1, and the rest was projections, transposes and XLA glue between small kernels. So we wrote the megakernel so that it covers the whole layer in 2 kernel dispatch, which made decode 25% faster at batch 8. The sparse attention kernel keep a layer’s working weights in SBUF, distributing weighted streaming across the cores and handling the interchip communication within There’s an approximation in the sparse-attention prefill, affecting about 1.2% of block selections. You can refer to the write-up for the profiling results: https://runanywhere.ai/blog/glm-5-3-flash-trainium2-nki-mega... Please give it a try yourself on a trn2.48xlarge and reproduce the AgentX results by following the steps in docs/RESULTS.md. Happy to collaborate and hear any feedback. Deploying high performant dedicated inference at lab like performance and half the price for open models such as the GLM-5.3 family, Kimi K3, Deepseek flash etc. is how we make money. You can talk to us regarding the same at founders@runanywhere.ai. We hope you find this useful. If you are working with Trainium or have experience with NKI kernels, we'd love to get your honest feedback. Feel free to share the models you want support for next, and we welcome any contributions to the repository.

title: Data Contracts
author: Martin Fowler (martin@martinfowler.com)
text: Data contracts are a way to describe the contents and guarantees of datasets. Simon Harrer and Arif Wider describe in detail what they are and how to use them. They apply practices from API design to data by treating them as data-providing services - such as data products - whose interfaces we want to define as clearly as possible. This approach significantly increases the robustness of large-scale data landscapes, and gives both people and AI agents the explicit, trustworthy metadata they need to work with data autonomously, which is why more and more enterprises are adopting them. more…

title: Globalna awaria Microsoft 365
text: Wstępny raport udostępniono klientom w centrum administracyjnym, a jego skróconą wersję na X zamieścił Charles Lamanna, wiceprezes Microsoftu odpowiedzialny za Copilota, agentów i platformę. Wynika z niej, że awarię wywołała kombinacja nieodkrytego defektu w oprogramowaniu, zmiany w ruchu i braku dostępności części serwerów. Raport końcowy ma się ukazać jeszcze w tym tygodniu. Według wstępnego raportu Microsoftu awaria zakłócała działanie usług od 12 listopada (godz. 16:20 UTC) do 13 listopada (godz. 16:10 UTC). Komunikat o pełnym przywróceniu działania opublikowano 14 listopada. Według doniesień problemy zgłaszano w ponad 70 krajach i terytoriach, a w Wielkiej Brytanii zakłóciły one pracę sektora ochrony zdrowia i innych usług publicznych. Dlaczego defekt przez ponad trzy miesiące nikomu nie przeszkadzał, a testy go nie wychwyciły? Co złożyło się na awarię? Wszystko działo się w bramie sieciowej, czyli zestawie serwerów, przez który przechodzi ruch do wielu usług Microsoft 365. Ani sama awaria, ani poprawka do niej nie dotyczą szerszych wdrożeń Windowsa. Defekt w poprawce W lipcu na serwery bramy trafiła poprawka przygotowana specjalnie dla nich. Przeszła przez procedurę bezpiecznego wdrażania i przez kilka tygodni objęła całą flotę serwerów. Przez ponad trzy miesiące nikt nie zauważył żadnych problemów. Okazało się jednak, że poprawka wprowadziła ukryty defekt. Przy określonym obciążeniu serwery przestawały odpowiadać. Przyczyną była rywalizacja o dostęp (lock contention) wewnątrz procesu: równoległe operacje konkurowały o dostęp do zasobów chronionych blokadami, co w określonych warunkach prowadziło do utraty responsywności serwera. Przełączenie ruchu Teams Microsoft utrzymuje dwa niezależne, odmienne systemy bram sieciowych, aby awaria jednego nie paraliżowała całej usługi. Około 15 godzin przed awarią ruch Teams został przełączony z alternatywnej bramy sieciowej na główną, obsługującą również Exchange Online. Lamanna zaznacza, że takie przełączenie to normalna część usługi. Zwiększyło to jednak ruch w głównej bramie i zmieniło jego charakter. Niedostępne 14% mocy serwerowej W czasie awarii niemal 14% mocy serwerowej bramy pozostawało niedostępne z powodu odrębnego problemu z poprzedniego dnia. Microsoft nie podał jego szczegółów. Według Microsoftu zapas wydajności był wystarczający, więc sama niedostępność tej części infrastruktury nie powodowała zakłóceń. Globalna awaria Gdy zbiegły się zwiększony ruch i ograniczona dostępna moc serwerowa, w bramie ujawnił się defekt z lipca. Żądania zaczęły się piętrzyć, aż serwery przestały odpowiadać. Stało się to w szczycie ruchu w Stanach. Potem zadziałał efekt domina. Kiedy serwer przestawał odpowiadać, system kierowania ruchem przekierowywał użytkowników do sprawnych serwerów, co normalnie chroni przed przerwami. Tym razem przekierowany ruch trafiał na kolejne serwery i wywoływał ten sam problem. W niecałe dwie godziny wada ujawniła się w całej flocie, a w najgorszym momencie ponad 80% serwerów tej bramy sieciowej nie odpowiadało. Rozlaniu awarii miały zapobiec przegrody między częściami infrastruktury. Standardowo brama składa się z tysięcy jednostek obliczeniowych (tzw. jednostek pojemności), zgrupowanych w regiony, a między nimi działają bariery, które mają zatrzymać taki lawinowy upadek. Z powodu osobnego problemu tym razem nie zatrzymały go i awaria objęła cały świat. Różne usługi, różny czas przywracania Nie wszystkie usługi padły na tak samo długo. Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint i aplikacje Office potrafią odłączyć się z uszkodzonej bramy, dzięki czemu ich działanie częściowo przywrócono wcześniej, a czaty i spotkania w Teams działały przez większą część awarii. Exchange Online nie mógł skorzystać z takiego przełączenia ze względu na skalę usługi. Awaria widoczna była też poza ekosystemem Microsoftu. Jak zauważył Antyweb, przestały działać wtyczki łączące usługi Microsoftu z ChatGPT i Claude’em. Dlaczego naprawa trwała tak długo? Serwery, które wracały do życia, od razu dostaw

title: Launch HN: StarSling (YC P25) – Self-improving CI for agent-volume repos
author: yonasb
text: We’re Yonas and Daniel and we’re building StarSling ( https://starsling.dev ), fast GitHub Actions runners with AI agents that ship PRs to continuously improve your tests and workflows. Every CI job gets its own ephemeral sandbox on the fastest Zen 5 machines and NVMe Disk with unlimited concurrency so a burst of agent PRs all run at once. We’re different from other runners because ours come with agents that cut down your CI bill over time. PRs are generated through our CI harness, which runs an agent loop that’s tuned to improve your CI speed and reduce cost. Mastra now merges over 1,800 PRs a month and we got their slowest workflow from 29m 56s on GitHub-hosted runners down to 5m 06s (5.87x) on StarSling. We realized the true value of having an agent loop running on top of fast runners when our agents found an 11-month-old performance bottleneck in better-auth. The fix made one of their test jobs 5.4x faster: https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/10762 . I previously founded StackShare, which grew to over 1.5M developers. Daniel helped build Netflix's internal developer portal. Last year we started building AI agents for DevOps because shipping code to prod fell way behind agentic coding. We hit the CI bottleneck ourselves as we were building agents. Our own agents shipped so many PRs that at peak our job queues were backed up for hours and our CI bill got close to our inference bill. We now support per-second billing, and just shipped StarSling Disks - persistent disks that give you a 4.9x speedup in dependencies ready over actions/cache. You can see a quick demo of disks in action here : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2JrrpRm9Mww . Our CI harness runs a loop that has agents: - Analyze your workflows, run logs, and machine telemetry - Propose an optimization - Test your unchanged workflow side by side the proposed change - Deterministically judge that the difference is statistically significant - Ship the winner to you as a PR with benchmarks evidence We benchmarked open source repos on our runners and average 10x speedup in wall clock time with 70% less runner time: - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-gogs (12.8x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-shellcheck (5.5x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-chatwoot (3.9x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-transfer.sh (11.7x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-mirotalksfu (36.4x) Yes, you can do these optimizations yourself with prompts so we’ve released skills for this: https://github.com/starslingdev/skills . The benefit of using our agents is that you don’t need to spend tokens and CI compute finding optimizations yourself. We started building our runners on AWS at the beginning of the year and realized that was too expensive. But at that time there weren’t any cloud providers that could give us the same machines we were getting on AWS, billed per minute (microVMs). So we convinced a handful of sandbox providers to get Zen 5s and started benchmarking them publicly ( https://github.com/starslingdev/hpc-sandbox-benchmarks ). We’ve learned that fast infrastructure is table stakes for CI, but it’s not sufficient on its own. To get fast and cost effective CI you need a process that continues making improvements. We turned CI optimizations from OpenAI, Anthropic, Linear and others into playbooks for your agent: https://starsling.dev/ci-playbooks . To try it, give your agent this URL: https://docs.starsling.dev/start . You get 2,000 free minutes. Our agents start opening PRs once you've hit about 10,000 minutes. Today we announced our CI Challenge: if StarSling can't save you at least 10% on your next CI bill, we'll literally give you $1,000. Eligibility and rules here: https://starsling.dev/blog/ci-challenge . We’d love your feedback on the headless experience and what you’d like to see improved in your own CI setup! https://starsling.dev

title: Software factories and code reviews with Harjot Gill
author: Gergely Orosz
text: Listen and watch now on YouTube , Apple , and Spotify . See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom. Brought to You by • turbopuffer – a ridiculously scalable, fast and cheap hybrid search engine, built on top of object storage, used by cutting-edge companies like Anthropic, Linear, Ramp and many others. Many companies that switch to turbopuffer are cutting their search bills by 50% or more and getting much faster results. Check it out. • Entire – Entire launched its own Git forge, shipped Continuous Memory, and reinvented the pull request (called Trails ). Trails are a much more natural workflow when agents keep pushing new changes, after iterating on feedback – and you have more context and control on when a change is ready to merge. Check it out • WorkOS – WorkOS built Airlock, the authorization layer for AI agents. It evaluates every request against the agent’s intent + your rules, and either allows it, denies it, or routes it to a human. Works with Claude Code, Codex & MCP gateways. Learn more In this episode In this conversation, we step into the world of an AI-pilled CEO to explore how their startup works. This episode might as well be a way of succeeding that contradicts the growing convention that AI spending costs are too high and must be clamped down on. Harjot Gill is founder and CEO of CodeRabbit , an AI code review business, and he shipped over 5,000 pull requests last month, spending on AI at a monthly run rate of $250,000(!) It’s certainly not a conventional approach and Harjot gets into detail about the thinking and reasoning behind it. In this episode of The Pragmatic Engineer Podcast , we talk about his background in building software and founding infra startups for the last 30 years, and how things changed into the era of building software factories at CodeRabbit. We talk about why he believes human code review is dead, and how his team maintains quality while shipping at unprecedented speed. We also get into the rising costs of AI development, why Harjot is convinced that tech startups need more funding than ever, and how AI is changing recruitment and the skills for success. Takeaways from the conversation with Harjot 1. Janitorial work formed a large part of his 5,000 PRs last month, pushed with agents. He sets off his agents to improve systems like the CI, fixing flaky tests, and refining caching. A lot of the PRs are generated during his commute, and at evenings and nights. In a few cases, he steers agents to make the UI feel better. Examples of stuff Harjot has built: A write-ahead log (WAL) on top of object stores using Rust (the agent ran for six weeks!). This WAL is now in production. Migrating all of CodeRabbit’s services over to Bun – running over a weekend A new CI system after the previous one had performance issues 2. CodeRabbit spends millions of dollars per month on AI, with a team of 40 engineers. Harjot estimates that a PR costs him around $150 in a personal spend of around $250-$275K per month. He compares it to marketing teams with 10 marketers at VC-funded companies who can drive $100M in spend. I point out that his startup is an outlier; the AI spend I hear about elsewhere is in the region of between $200-$2,000 per month, per dev . Finding out how this spend makes sense was one reason I was keen to meet Harjot. 3. For dev tooling startups like CodeRabbit, massive AI spend can be justified by launching new, AI-related products faster. It feels to me that CodeRabbit is not a typical company: its AI spending is a form of R&D if it creates new solutions that can be commercialized and sold. It’s not the same at places with fixed customer bases willing to pay a certain amount for an existing product, and no more. Also, Harjot says that they got quoted $13M/year for a CI solution to handle their PR output, but the price made him decide they’d build their own CI system using agents. It took a week, and the new CI cost 50% less than the quot

title: Launch HN: Maritime (YC F26) – A managed cloud for production AI agents
author: ashriv
text: Hi HN, we're Ary and Maria, co-founders of Maritime ( https://maritime.sh ). We're building an agent-native cloud that handles everything from custom environments to lifecycle management for AI agents. Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lCWMdBQ96rY There’s been an explosion of sandbox companies coming out of SF, but sandboxes solve maybe 10% of the infrastructure problem for AI agents. The approach that most sandboxing companies take is: You buy Hetzner/OVH Cloud bare metal servers, use Firecracker to slice the servers up into VMs, sell those VMs with low margins. It’s a bit of an oversimplification, but the point is it’s a narrow solution to a fairly difficult problem. We talked to a couple hundred companies that are building AI agents. From personal assistants and coding agents to specialized healthcare agents, and the main pattern we saw was that even after choosing a sandbox provider, you still have to build additional infrastructure just to get things working. These were the primary points of friction: 1. Agent lifecycle management. There’s a lot that you have to build in order to properly give your agents VMs: things like sleep/wake, persistent storage, triggers, scheduling, per-user routing and spend caps, health monitoring, failure recovery, and deploying updates across thousands of VMs without downtime. There are so many of these small sandbox management tasks that companies have to build and maintain themselves, and they add up. 2. Custom environments. Production agents have varying needs. Some agents need Windows applications. Others need Android, browsers with persistent sessions, custom operating system images, preinstalled desktop software and applications, or specific dependencies. Some agents need access to private networks to interact with customer-specific things on prem, or residential IPs, or the ability to restrict network access completely. 3. Cost optimization. If you’re selling a personal assistant for $20/month, a sandbox that costs $0.04/hour comes out to roughly $29/month if you keep it running continuously, not including LLM inference, storage, etc. There is a way to combat this though, which is to optimize sandbox usage with auto-snapshotting, making things event-driven, mounting S3 buckets to agent environments via FUSE for cheap storage, cold-tiering snapshots, etc. All roads lead to… building more infrastructure. So what did we build differently? We give each agent its own isolated, persistent microVM and a configurable environment. On top of the compute, we built a lot of composable services: provisioning, persistent state, sleep/wake orchestration, triggers, schedule creation, monitoring, network configuration, updates, rollbacks, recovery, per-agent spend tracking, login handoffs, all the things you’d need for production agents. We also spent a huge amount of time optimizing cost. A lot of thought was put into things such as scale-to-zero, copy-on-write over shared base images, compressed memory snapshots, hot/warm/cold snapshot and disk tiering, and other optimizations while balancing these with performance metrics like latency. As a result, Maritime costs $1 for a 2gb RAM agent per month (unlimited usage for that $1), with additional resources available as needed. Maria was a visiting lecturer at MIT and did research at Project NANDA on agent infrastructure. Ary did research on agent coordination protocols at the same lab. We started Maritime together this March because of all the issues we faced with trying to deploy agents to the cloud during our research. We want your feedback. If you're building an agent product, what did you have to build on top of sandboxes to make them work? We want to know about all the workarounds and weird things you’ve had to build. Are there things you’ve tried to build with VMs but couldn’t? Does Maritime fit your needs? Is there a feature we’re missing that would make us more enticing? Happy to answer any questions in the comments. https://maritime.sh

title: Show HN: Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we use to build Mastra
author: codekarate
text: Hi HN, we're Shane, Sam, and Abhi. Almost two years ago, we shared Mastra, our open-source TypeScript agent framework, on Show HN: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43103073 . It got a few hundred upvotes; a couple of weeks later our downloads had doubled, and we were off to the races. Today we're sharing Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we built to help maintain Mastra itself. At Mastra, we now average nearly 4M downloads per week, and with Factory our team now merges hundreds of PRs a week across the mastra-ai GitHub org. Last week, Factory opened and merged 238 PRs, alongside 630 merged PRs from humans. There's a lot of debate about what a software factory is. For us Factory is a configurable agentic kanban board that's @-taggable in Slack. Under the hood, it uses Mastra’s durable agents for long-running sessions, our conversational memory system, a markdown based wiki with source citations to incorporate company knowledge, signals that subscribe to PR comments wired up into sessions, and a customizable cloud sandbox with our coding harness (working on supporting Claude Code, Codex etc). When we started out, we modeled Factory around our existing workflow-oriented process (triage, plan, build, review, shipped). Three months later, we find ourselves mostly driving it through Slack vs a web UI. We’ve seen more senior engineers kick off sessions in parallel (“triage the 20 oldest issues and let’s evaluate…”). We’re using bug and vuln scanners now, and we’ve closed our repo to outside contributors, asking folks to write detailed issue repros instead. You can get started with `npm create factory`. It’s fully open-source, so you can run it entirely on your infra (we also offer a hosted version). Comment here, we would love to know what you think! https://factory.mastra.ai https://github.com/mastra-ai/template-factory
